title: The Last Man on Earth

evidence.note: The two Internet Archive items carry different labels. TheLastManOnEarthHD has a Public Domain Mark 1.0 license URL and TheLastManOnEarth_72 has a CC0 1.0 license URL (checked in the items' metadata). Both are uploader labels, not rights determinations. The film was released in the US in 1964. For works first published 1964–1977, the Copyright Renewal Act of 1992 made renewal automatic, so a missed renewal cannot by itself have put a 1964 US film into the public domain. Any public domain status would therefore have to rest on a failure of the copyright notice, and no document establishing that was located in this session. The common claim online that the film was lost through a failure to renew is not supported by this reading.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office — Circular 15a: Duration of Copyright

evidence.note: The film is credited as a US–Italian co-production. The URAA (1994) restored US copyright for eligible foreign works still protected in their home country, even where US protection had been lost through a formality failure. Whether the work counts as an eligible foreign work, and what its Italian term was, was not verified in this session, so the restoration question is unresolved.
evidence.source: Cornell University Library — Copyright & Fair Use: Public Domain (URAA section)

evidence.note: This is a sound film, and its recorded score normally shares the film print's copyright status, so the score layer follows the unresolved print layer. No separate score registration was located in this session.

The Internet Archive metadata for the film says it is based on Richard Matheson's novel "I am Legend". The novel is a separate copyrighted work that is treated as still in force. Under Stewart v. Abend, a derivative work cannot be exploited during the underlying work's copyright term without the owner's permission, so the source story can restrict reuse of the film whatever the print's status. The novel's registration and renewal records were not pulled in this session.
evidence.source: Stewart v. Abend, 495 U.S. 207 (1990) — Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute

evidence.note: No trademark registration for the title or related franchise names was checked in this session. The source novel has been adapted commercially more than once, so avoid franchise naming in titles or branding.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
The Internet Archive HD item's metadata describes the upload as an HD restoration. Modern HD remasters can carry new protectable elements.

editorial:
The Last Man on Earth (1964) is a science fiction horror film starring Vincent Price as Dr. Robert Morgan, the only healthy survivor of a plague that has turned the rest of humanity into night-dwelling creatures. The Internet Archive metadata credits Ubaldo Ragona and Sidney Salkow as directors and says it is based on Richard Matheson's novel "I am Legend". It is widely circulated online. Two Internet Archive items host it, one labeled HD and one a separate upload. They carry different free-use labels: Public Domain Mark 1.0 on the HD item and CC0 1.0 on the other.

The rights trap has two parts. First, the print's free status is unconfirmed. Those labels are uploader designations. Because renewal became automatic in 1992 for works published from 1964 to 1977, the popular explanation that the film lapsed through a missed renewal does not hold up, and any public domain claim would have to rest on a notice failure that this research did not document. The film's US–Italian co-production origin also leaves a possible URAA restoration question open. Second, Matheson's novel is a separate work still treated as protected. Under Stewart v. Abend, a new commercial adaptation or reuse of the story can require a license from the novel's owner even if the print itself were free.
faq: The film is hosted everywhere as public domain. Is that confirmed?

No. The Internet Archive's Public Domain Mark and CC0 labels are uploader designations. Renewal was automatic for works published 1964–1977, so a missed renewal is not a route to public domain for this film. Only a failure of the copyright notice could be, and this research found no record showing that. The US–Italian co-production origin also leaves a URAA restoration claim unresolved.
Can I make a new adaptation based on this film?

Not without clearing the underlying novel. Richard Matheson's I Am Legend is a separate copyrighted work. Under Stewart v. Abend, its owner can restrict commercial use of a derivative film's story even if the film print is free to use.
